\section{Discussion and limitations}\label{sec:6}\ThesisCheckNumber{section}{6}

\subsection{Relating the findings to the literature}\label{sec:6.1}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{6.1}

The baseline findings are consistent with the existing literature, but only narrowly. Headey and Palloni \autocite*{HeadeyPalloni2019} find that, under a within-region panel design netting out time-invariant confounding, sanitation improvements predict large reductions in diarrhoea and mortality but are \textbf{not} associated with stunting or wasting, while improved water is statistically insignificant for most outcomes except piped water (reduced stunting). Their null sanitation--stunting finding parallels this thesis's own null household- and community-sanitation associations with HAZ (Sections 5.1--5.2): both find no detectable sanitation--growth association once a design better suited to netting out confounding is used, each in its own way (region-level panel fixed effects there; region or cluster fixed effects here, with no household-level fixed effect). This is narrower than claiming WASH--growth associations generally attenuate under better controls, which would overstate what any single study establishes.

The household cluster-fixed-effects associations (Table 5.1) are not significant at the 5\% level, broadly consistent with the strongest randomised evidence available: no WASH-only arm in the three trials showed a statistically detectable growth effect (Section 2.3), while the nutrition arm (no WASH component) showed a modest positive effect, and adding WASH to nutrition brought no additional benefit over nutrition alone \autocite{Cumming2019}. This is not confirmation: the exposure here is a facility-type classification in cross-sectional data, not a randomised intervention with prospective follow-up from birth, so the two literatures answer related but distinct questions. The one significant household-level result (Section 5.3) is negative and just below threshold, one cell among twelve in that table, not evidence that improved household water harms growth; no mechanism in Section 2 supports that reading.

The historical extension's pooled water--HAZ association is positive and significant (Section 5.6), independently reproduced with a second estimation library on a separately rebuilt sample, as were all 24 primary established-date cells (Appendix~B). Computational reproduction is not a multiplicity correction: no formal adjustment has been applied for the number of cells estimated across the baseline and historical analyses, so this thesis has neither quantified nor ruled out the possibility that this result is one significant draw among many tested cells. It would be tempting to read the coefficient as evidence that introducing a time dimension recovers an association that the single-round baseline design cannot detect. Section 6.2 explains why this thesis does not draw that conclusion.

\subsection{Why baseline and historical results cannot test exposure timing}\label{sec:6.2}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{6.2}

This point has its own subsection because it is the most tempting overinterpretation that the structure of this thesis invites. The research question of the historical extension (Sections 1.2 and 1.3) is framed deliberately to avoid it: the extension asks whether modelled early-life local WASH coverage is associated with outcomes \emph{within its own sample}, not whether assigning a historical rather than a current exposure changes an otherwise identical estimate.

The baseline and historical samples differ in at least four respects at the same time, not in one:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Different children and survey rounds.} The baseline uses 2022--2025 DHS rounds from four countries; the historical extension uses 2014--2018 rounds from three, with Ethiopia's 2016 round entering only as a provisional sensitivity analysis outside the established-date pooled sample (Section 1.4). No child appears in both samples.
\item
  \textbf{Different exposure definitions and construction.} The baseline household exposure is each child's own household's survey response; the community exposure is an unweighted leave-one-out proportion among other classifiable HR responses in the same cluster, not a census of it (Section 3.3). The historical exposure is a modelled, area-averaged, annual gridded coverage estimate from an external source (IHME), matched to a specific postnatal window (Sections 3.5 to 3.7) --- a different kind of measurement, not the same quantity at a different time.
\item
  \textbf{Different eligibility and completion rules.} The historical sample also requires complete spatial coverage and a complete exposure window verified against the interview date (Section 3.7), with no counterpart in the baseline sample.
\item
  \textbf{Different control sets and identifying variation.} The main baseline household specification uses cluster fixed effects with household- and individual-level socioeconomic controls (Section 3.4); region fixed effects appear in the region-fixed-effects and community specifications (Sections 4.1, 4.3, 4.4) but are never stacked with the household model's cluster fixed effects. The historical specification uses cluster fixed effects with country-by-birth-year terms, excludes wealth for a reason specific to its design (Sections 3.8, 4.6), and is identified by genuine within-cluster variation across birth cohorts. The baseline community model is deliberately not estimated with cluster fixed effects, for a reason specific to its leave-one-out construction (Section 4.3) with no bearing on the historical design.
\end{enumerate}

Because all four differ at once, a contrast between the baseline's largely null associations and the historical extension's selected pooled water--HAZ headline cannot be cleanly attributed to ``the effect of assigning historical instead of current exposure'' --- that headline is one of six nominally significant cells among the 24 primary cells, not the only significant historical result (Section 5.6). The contrast could instead, or in addition, reflect different confounding structures across the two country sets, different measurement-error properties of a modelled surface versus a survey response, the different control sets, or chance given the number of cells estimated (the multiplicity point of Section 5.6 applies here too). No formal test of the baseline-versus-historical difference was carried out, and a significant coefficient beside non-significant ones does not by itself show the two differ significantly. This thesis does not adjudicate between these explanations: its design, two separately constructed samples rather than one shared sample in which only exposure timing varies, cannot do so.

\textbf{What the within-historical-sample window comparison does and does not hold constant.} Section 5.7 compares four exposure windows (birth year, prenatal, post-12-month and post-24-month) within the \emph{same} historical country set and estimation approach. The comparison holds constant the survey rounds, the exposure source and spatial-extraction method, the control set and the estimator. In terms of specification, it changes only which months of the IHME surface are averaged into each child's exposure value. It does \textbf{not} hold the estimation sample constant across the four windows: each window has its own eligible sample, which differs according to which children have complete coverage for that specific window (Section 5.7). Table 5.7 shows how much this can matter. With the window held at post-12-month, the estimate moves from 1.03 on its own eligible sample to 1.64 on the smaller sample eligible under all four windows, a change in sample composition rather than in the window. Differences between the own-sample window estimates therefore combine window changes and sample-composition changes. The window comparison also says nothing about the baseline-versus-historical contrast discussed above, and this paragraph keeps the two separate.

\subsection{Limitations: unresolved documentation}\label{sec:6.3}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{6.3}

Two issues in the historical extension remain genuinely unresolved documentation gaps, neither a design choice nor an inherent limitation. First, no DHS or IPUMS source documents a measurement-subsample or anthropometry-specific sampling weight, despite repeated attempts (Appendix A records the sources tried); this thesis's working inference, not a documented fact, is that within-survey PERWEIGHT normalisation removes a constant measurement-subsample selection factor under random household-level selection, though it cannot correct for differential non-response among eligible but unmeasured children. Second, the gap between Nigeria 2018's official count of measured children (12,806) and the IPUMS birth-history extract's non-missing-anthropometry count (11,704) remains unexplained (Section 3.9).

Both points bear on which children the historical estimates describe, so this thesis reports its historical coefficients as \textbf{weighted conditional associations among eligible measured children}, not population-representative estimates. Reporting the unweighted estimate alongside (Section 5.6) does not resolve this, since the selection question is who was measured at all, not how measured children are weighted; if measurement or non-response related to both local WASH coverage and growth, the estimated associations could differ from the full eligible population in a direction the data cannot show.

\subsection{Limitations: authorised design choices}\label{sec:6.4}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{6.4}

Three features of the design are deliberate, disclosed choices, not errors.

First, the equal-country-total pooled weighting (Section 4.5) gives each established-date country equal total observation weight in a single pooled regression, not a population-size-weighted estimate or an average of each country's separately estimated coefficient: statistical influence on the pooled slope also depends on residualized exposure variation after controls, so equal weight totals do not imply equal influence. This consequence is disclosed throughout: the pooled water--HAZ coefficient moves from 1.03 (weighted) to 0.41 (unweighted, same observations); neither is population-representative (Section 3.8).

Second, the working 12-month postnatal exposure window was chosen during the design phase, before any model was estimated, for a documented reason: it is an early-life window whose completion can be checked against the interview date. It is nowhere described in this thesis as ``preregistered''. The literature basis for this specific window length is modest. Cumming and Cairncross \autocite*{CummingCairncross2016} support early-life exposure in general and, if anything, lean toward a 24-month window, which is why all four candidate windows (Section 5.7) are reported together.

Third, wealth quintile is excluded from the historical extension's main specification because it may be a post-exposure mediator of historical WASH conditions, correlated with the exposure itself (Section 3.8), a substantive identification concern, not a claim that cluster fixed effects remove wealth mechanically (Section 4.2 shows otherwise). Section 3.8 also states the competing concern: current wealth may proxy earlier socioeconomic circumstances that confound the association, left unaddressed if wealth is excluded. Adding wealth leaves the pooled water--HAZ coefficient essentially unchanged (1.01 vs.~1.03; Section 5.8), but this sensitivity does not adjudicate between the two readings.

\subsection{Limitations: inherent, not resolvable}\label{sec:6.5}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{6.5}

DHS/IHME input overlap affects two of the three established-date historical countries, Ghana and Kenya, whose own DHS surveys feed into the IHME gridded estimates used as the exposure. The exposure measure is therefore not fully independent of the survey data used in the analysis. This thesis reports the overlap-exclusion sensitivity alongside the main estimate rather than treating the overlap as removable: the pooled water--HAZ estimate excluding Ghana is 0.74 (Section 5.8). Because that estimate pools Kenya and Nigeria, Kenya's overlap remains in it, so the sensitivity addresses only part of the overlap.

Current residence, as recorded at the survey date, is used as a proxy for residence during each child's early-life window. Children whose survey residence differs from their early-life residence may be assigned an exposure that does not represent their early-life location, under both the primary buffer-average method and the containing-pixel sensitivity. This is a form of exposure measurement error whose extent in these samples is unknown.

DHS cluster coordinates are randomly displaced for confidentiality (Section 3.4), and this limitation holds whatever extraction method is used: the primary buffer average and the containing-pixel sensitivity (Section 5.8) both read pixels around the displaced coordinates, through different mechanisms, and neither recovers the true location or corrects for the undisclosed displacement DHS actually applied (Sections 3.5--3.6).

The IHME exposure surface is itself a \emph{modelled} estimate with its own uncertainty, not a direct observation; its supplied lower and upper bounds are not used as regression inputs, so the standard errors of the historical coefficients do not reflect uncertainty in the exposure surface itself. The surface's annual resolution also means the value used for a window's final touched year can include months after the child's own interview date even once the postnatal completion rule (Section 3.7) is satisfied; the project's construction flags every such case but neither excludes nor adjusts for it (Section 3.7).

The residual within-cluster exposure variation that actually identifies the historical coefficients is small (0.20 to 0.88 percentage points depending on country and product, Section 4.6; 0.43 for the pooled water--HAZ model, Section 5.6) --- modest relative to the 10-point reporting scale, which is a convention, not a description of a change typically observed within a cluster. Finally, Ethiopia's interview-date uncertainty (Section 5.9; Appendix~C) is an inherent limitation of that round's recoded date fields, not a design choice; its estimates remain provisional and outside the established-date pooled family.

\subsection{What this thesis does not claim}\label{sec:6.6}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{6.6}

This thesis does not claim its findings establish a causal effect of WASH facilities on child growth, in either direction: both analyses are cross-sectional and observational, and fixed effects remove only what is shared within a region or cluster, leaving within-cluster confounding possible (Section 4.2). Nor does it read the null or weak baseline associations as evidence that WASH investment is an ineffective use of development resources, generalise findings from these four countries to Sub-Saharan Africa as a region (Section 1.4), treat computational verification (Appendix~B) as evidence of improved causal identification, or, per Section 6.2, treat the baseline/historical contrast as evidence that exposure timing explains it.
